comparison: Perfect agreement on claims C90-C92. Both evaluations support the acknowledgment that successful performance can occur without task-anchored grid firing and that alternative mechanisms exist. Both note the speculative nature of alternative mechanisms (C91-C92), with OpenEval marking as UNCERTAIN and peer reviewers accepting this as consistent with the correlative nature of the study.

Strong agreement on claims C26-C28 regarding grid cell identification methodology. Both evaluations support these basic characterization claims without question. OpenEval also includes C110 (quantitative results) which peer reviewers do not explicitly address but implicitly accept.

Strong agreement on claims C6, C56-C57, C59-C60, C87 regarding behavioral differences between task-anchored and task-independent conditions on uncued trials. Both evaluations treat this as a central, well-supported finding. OpenEval emphasizes statistical support from mixed-effects models; peer reviewers describe it as 'convincing evidence.'

Agreement on claims C68-C69 distinguishing current findings from prior work (Low et al., 2021). Both evaluations support this distinction. OpenEval also includes C67 (limitation about not recording all grid cells simultaneously), which peer reviewers address separately in R3.

Strong agreement on claims C55, C58, C78 regarding no performance difference on beaconed trials between conditions. Both evaluations support this dissociation as key evidence. Peer review also includes C79 (broader interpretation about selective enhancement), which OpenEval addresses in R9.

Partial agreement on claims C54, C64, C70-C71 regarding non-grid cell heterogeneity. OpenEval supports these observations but notes C72 is speculative. Peer reviewers mark as UNCERTAIN, specifically questioning the behavioral relevance and functional significance of distinct non-grid populations, indicating this requires further investigation.

Both address the core dual coding finding (C2, C62). OpenEval groups C2, C62, C65-C66 together as the main finding, marking as SUPPORTED. Peer review focuses on C2, C29-C31, C62 and also marks as SUPPORTED, with all reviewers explicitly accepting this classification. Both treat the dual modes as well-established.

Both address periodogram analysis and firing mode classification (C29-C31). OpenEval evaluates C29-C38 as SUPPORTED based on Lomb-Scargle analysis. Peer review includes C29-C31 with C2, C62 as the accepted core finding. Both agree the classification methodology is sound.

Both address coherent switching among grid cells (C47-C48, C53). OpenEval marks as SUPPORTED with acknowledgment of limitation (C67). Peer review also supports the coherent switching observation, noting population-level coordination. Both accept the attractor dynamics interpretation without challenge.

Both address within-session switching (C39, C41-C42). OpenEval marks as SUPPORTED based on rolling window analysis, noting limited temporal resolution. Peer review accepts the switching observation as a strength but raises UNCERTAIN evaluation regarding temporal causality - whether activity anchoring or behavior changed first. This represents a key difference in interpretation.

Both reference block structure claims (C40, C45). OpenEval supports the non-random block structure (p=0.0003). Peer review marks as UNCERTAIN, specifically questioning the causal direction and temporal relationship between neural switching and behavioral changes. This is a substantive disagreement about interpretation.

Both address the main conclusion about grid cells and path integration (C61, C88). OpenEval marks as SUPPORTED, integrating behavioral and neural findings. Peer review also supports this, with reviewers describing it as 'a significant step toward better understanding' grid cell contributions to behavior. Both treat the selective enhancement interpretation positively.

Overlapping coverage of behavioral-neural correlation (C63). OpenEval includes C63 in broader conclusion (C61, C63, C79-C80, C88) marked as SUPPORTED. Peer review includes C63 in the central finding about uncued trial performance (C6, C56-C57, C59-C60, C63, C87) also marked as SUPPORTED. Strong agreement.

OpenEval evaluates claims C76-C77 as UNCERTAIN, noting C76 (intact cued performance during task-independent firing) is reasonable but C77 (speculative mechanisms) lacks direct evidence. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these specific mechanistic speculation claims.

OpenEval evaluates claims C95-C97 as UNCERTAIN, supporting C95 (variability in grid cell anchoring) but noting C96-C97 are speculative about underlying mechanisms without direct evidence. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these mechanism-focused claims.

OpenEval evaluates claims C102-C109 (experimental methods) as SUPPORTED, noting clear description with appropriate controls. Peer reviewers do not provide a separate evaluation of these methodological claims, though methods are implicitly accepted.
OpenEval evaluates claims C22-C25 (prior work summary and knowledge gap) as SUPPORTED. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these literature context claims.

OpenEval evaluates claims C12-C19 (prior experimental work and limitations of perturbation approaches) as SUPPORTED. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these background literature claims.
OpenEval evaluates claims C83-C86 (citations to prior work and speculation about other cell types) as SUPPORTED. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these contextual claims.

OpenEval evaluates claims C99-C101 (extensions to human cognition and clinical populations) as UNCERTAIN, noting reasonable speculation but no direct evidence from current study. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these translational speculation claims.

Minimal overlap on claims C49-C51 regarding non-grid cell behavior. OpenEval groups these with C47-C48, C52-C53 about grid cell coherent switching, marking as SUPPORTED. Peer review groups C49-C51 with C4, C54, C64, C70-C71 about non-grid heterogeneity, marking as UNCERTAIN regarding behavioral relevance. Different grouping reflects different analytical focus.
